Swarthy

/SWOR-thee/ - the stress falls on SWOR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Swarthy means having a dark complexion.

The opera's costume notes call for a swarthy pirate king, his dark complexion set off by a scarlet coat.

Worked Example

In the memoir, the author's swarthy uncle stands out in every photograph of the pale northern village — olive-skinned and dark-haired, the one face the neighbors never mistook for anyone else's.

Swarthy is a literary, slightly old-fashioned word for having a dark complexion. It describes coloring only — most often in ballads, novels, and old records — and says nothing about character; modern writing outside such contexts usually just says 'dark-skinned' or 'tanned.'

How Swarthy Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

dusky

dusky: dark-toned, often poetic, used of light and skin alike

tanned

tanned: darkened by the sun, usually temporarily

Antonyms

fair

fair: light in coloring

pale

pale: lacking color, sometimes from illness

How Strong Is It? — fair → tanned → swarthy

fair vs. swarthy

fair vs. swarthy: Fair names the lightest coloring on this scale, as far from swarthy as a complexion can be — the pale end of the ladder.

tanned vs. swarthy

tanned vs. swarthy: Tanned is darkness the sun lends and winter takes back; it stops short of swarthy, which names a complexion that is naturally deep-toned.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — swarth

Root — swarth: dark, dusky (Old English sweart, 'black')

Suffix — -y

Suffix — -y: characterized by

Put it together

Put it together: Old English sweart meant 'black, dark' — the same ancient Germanic word that became modern German schwarz. English kept it as swart, added -y, 'characterized by,' and swarthy has meant 'dark-complexioned' since the 1500s. This is the unit's one true example of its title suffix: dark + -y = characterized by darkness.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Sweart faded out of everyday English centuries ago — swart survives only in dialect and old poetry — so swarthy has no living relative to lean on. Its closest kin is across the border in German, where schwarz is still the ordinary word for 'black.'

Strength Check

Word Choice

literary / dated

Swarthy belongs to ballads, sea novels, and old records — exactly where the SAT will show it to you. It describes complexion only. In your own writing, prefer 'dark-complexioned' or 'tanned'; reach for swarthy only when echoing that older literary voice.
